meta.author: bank-team-us-history
meta.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: A legal clerk's note asks how the assembly line changed factory output.

answer.exemplar: It broke production into simple repeated tasks, letting workers specialize and massively increasing output and lowering costs.

questions.explanation: Specialization and repetition boosted output and cut costs. It did not require skilled craftsmen for every step.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks what most influenced factory siting in the early twentieth century.

options.text: Access to power, transport, and labor pools
Proximity to royal palaces
Distance from all roads and rails
Presence of scenic mountain views

questions.explanation: Factories needed power, transport, and labor. Scenic views or isolation from transport were not drivers.

stimulus.body: A clerk quotes a reformer describing overcrowded tenements with poor ventilation and sanitation in immigrant neighborhoods.

questions.stem: What problem does that description highlight?

options.text: Excess suburban housing supply
Unsafe and unhealthy urban housing for the poor
Rural farmhouses lacking electricity
Luxury apartments for the wealthy

questions.explanation: The quote highlights unsafe, unhealthy urban housing. It does not describe suburbs, farms, or luxury housing.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks what the Immigration Act of 1924 established.

options.text: Mandatory citizenship for all residents
Open borders for all immigrants
National origins quotas favoring Northern and Western Europeans
Deportation of all foreign-born citizens

questions.explanation: The 1924 act imposed national origins quotas favoring Northern and Western Europeans. It did not open borders or mandate citizenship.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks how the Triangle Shirtwaist fire changed labor law.

answer.exemplar: The 1911 fire killed 146 workers and spurred workplace safety regulations and fire codes.

questions.explanation: The tragedy led to safety regulations and fire codes. It did not end factory work but improved conditions.

questions.stem: A clerk's debate asks why early factory safety laws were often weak.

options.text: Safety laws were banned by the Supreme Court
Workers unanimously opposed all safety rules
Factories already had perfect safety records
Business opposition and limited enforcement resources

questions.explanation: Business resistance and weak enforcement limited early laws. Workers wanted safety, and records were not perfect.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks how installment credit affected 1920s consumerism.

answer.exemplar: It let consumers buy goods over time, boosting demand and production but increasing household debt.

questions.explanation: Installment plans expanded consumption and debt. They did not reduce debt or limit demand.

questions.stem: A clerk's table shows rising industrial output but stagnant farm incomes in the 1920s; what does this imply?
questions.explanation: The divergence shows prosperity was uneven, with industry thriving while agriculture lagged, masking underlying economic weakness.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks why buying stocks on margin was dangerous.

options.text: It required paying full price upfront
Borrowed money amplified losses when prices fell
It guaranteed profits regardless of market
It was illegal for all investors

questions.explanation: Margin buying amplified both gains and losses. It did not require full upfront payment or guarantee profits.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks why bank runs spread during the Depression.

answer.exemplar: Fear of insolvency led depositors to withdraw funds simultaneously, forcing banks to fail and deepening panic.

questions.explanation: Mass withdrawals created self-fulfilling failures. Deposit insurance later restored confidence.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks what the Social Security Act of 1935 created.

options.text: A military draft for unemployed men
Universal healthcare for all citizens
Federal pensions for the elderly and unemployment insurance
Abolition of all private pensions

questions.explanation: The act established pensions and unemployment insurance. It did not create universal healthcare or abolish private pensions.

questions.topic: Deficit spending in the New Deal
questions.stem: A clerk's note asks why New Deal programs used deficit spending.

answer.exemplar: Government spent more than it collected to stimulate demand and create jobs during the Depression.

questions.explanation: Deficit spending aimed to boost demand and employment. It was not accidental or purely wasteful.

questions.learningObjective: Analyze judicial resistance to New Deal
questions.stem: A clerk's note asks why the Supreme Court struck down early New Deal laws.

options.text: It abolished the presidency
It supported all New Deal programs unanimously
It ruled the Depression was fictional
It viewed federal economic regulation as exceeding constitutional limits

questions.explanation: The Court saw federal economic regulation as overreach. It did not deny the Depression or abolish the presidency.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks why Dust Bowl farmers migrated west.

answer.exemplar: Drought and soil erosion ruined farms, pushing families to seek work in California and elsewhere.

questions.explanation: Environmental collapse drove migration. It was not voluntary prosperity-seeking.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks what happened to U.S. factories during World War II.

options.text: They closed entirely for the war's duration
They shifted from consumer goods to military production
They produced only agricultural equipment
They moved all production overseas

questions.explanation: Factories converted to military production. They did not close or move overseas.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks what the GI Bill provided to veterans.

options.text: Automatic citizenship for foreign veterans
Lifetime exemption from all taxes
Education, housing, and unemployment benefits
Free automobiles for all veterans

questions.explanation: The GI Bill offered education, housing, and unemployment aid. It did not grant tax exemptions or cars.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks how World War II changed women's workforce participation.

answer.exemplar: Women entered industrial and defense jobs in large numbers, symbolized by Rosie the Riveter, though many left after the war.

questions.explanation: Wartime labor needs drew women into industry. Postwar expectations pushed many out again.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks what drove postwar suburban growth.

options.text: Abolition of mortgages
Collapse of all urban housing
Federal ban on city living
Highway construction, GI Bill loans, and white flight

questions.explanation: Highways, GI loans, and white flight fueled suburbs. There was no ban on city living or abolition of mortgages.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks how interstate highways affected urban centers.

answer.exemplar: They enabled suburban commuting and decentralized industry, drawing population and jobs away from city cores.

questions.explanation: Highways facilitated suburbanization and decentralization. They did not concentrate growth in city centers.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the baby boom's economic effect
questions.stem: A clerk's note asks how the baby boom affected the postwar economy.

options.text: It shrank the labor force permanently
It increased demand for housing, schools, and consumer goods
It ended all consumer spending
It caused immediate economic collapse

questions.explanation: The baby boom boosted demand for housing, schools, and goods. It did not shrink labor or end spending.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks what restrictive covenants did in housing markets.

answer.exemplar: They contractually barred non-white buyers from neighborhoods, enforcing residential segregation.

questions.explanation: Covenants excluded non-white buyers, reinforcing segregation. They were later struck down legally.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks what Brown v. Board of Education held.

options.text: Schools must be privatized
Segregation is permissible if facilities are equal
Racial segregation in public schools is unconstitutional
Only white students may attend public schools

questions.explanation: Brown held school segregation unconstitutional, overturning Plessy. It did not privatize schools or exclude Black students.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks what the Civil Rights Act of 1964 prohibited.

options.text: Segregation in the military only
Only racial discrimination in voting
All private speech and association
Discrimination in public accommodations and employment

questions.explanation: The 1964 Act barred discrimination in public accommodations and employment. It did not cover only voting or military.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks why African Americans moved north in the Great Migration.

answer.exemplar: They sought industrial jobs and escaped Jim Crow segregation and racial violence in the South.

questions.explanation: Economic opportunity and escape from segregation drove migration. It was not forced relocation.
questions.hint: Jobs and escape from Jim Crow.

questions.stem: A clerk's table shows rising factory productivity but falling factory jobs after 1970; what does this imply?
questions.explanation: Rising productivity with fewer jobs implies automation and efficiency gains displaced workers, not just demand collapse.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks why Northern industry declined after 1970.

answer.exemplar: Global competition, automation, and capital flight to lower-cost regions shrank Northern manufacturing.

questions.explanation: Competition, automation, and capital flight drove decline. It was not a single cause.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks what stagflation describes.

options.text: Rapid growth with zero inflation
High inflation combined with high unemployment
Deflation with full employment
Stable prices with rising wages only

questions.explanation: Stagflation combines high inflation and high unemployment. It defies the usual trade-off.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks what affirmative action aimed to do.

answer.exemplar: It sought to expand opportunities for historically disadvantaged groups in education and employment.

questions.explanation: Affirmative action aimed to broaden access for disadvantaged groups. It was not a quota for every position.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks what caused 1970s urban fiscal crises.

options.text: Complete absence of city governments
Surplus city revenues and low spending
Shrinking tax bases and rising service demands
Federal takeover of all city budgets

questions.explanation: Tax base erosion and rising demands caused fiscal crises. Cities were not abolished or fully federalized.

questions.topic: Industrial retention after a plant closing
questions.stem: A clerk's note asks what communities did to retain industry after plant closings.

options.text: Abolished local government services
Banned all new businesses from entering
Raised taxes to drive out remaining firms
Offered tax incentives and retraining programs

questions.explanation: Communities used tax incentives and retraining to retain industry. They did not raise taxes or abolish services.

questions.stem: A clerk's debate asks how assembly lines affected workers.

options.text: They eliminated all factory jobs immediately
They increased output but made work repetitive and deskilled
They required every worker to be a master craftsman
They ended mass production entirely

questions.explanation: Assembly lines raised output but deskilled work. They did not eliminate jobs or require master craftsmen.

stimulus.body: A clerk quotes a planner noting factories located near immigrant neighborhoods to tap cheap labor.

questions.stem: What does that siting pattern imply about labor markets?

options.text: Immigrants refused factory work
Factories avoided all workers
Employers sought accessible, low-cost labor pools
Labor was irrelevant to siting decisions

questions.explanation: Siting near immigrant neighborhoods shows employers sought cheap accessible labor. Labor was central to siting.

questions.stem: A clerk synthesizes how tenement reform changed urban housing.

answer.exemplar: Reforms introduced light, air, and sanitation standards, gradually improving conditions though overcrowding persisted.

questions.explanation: Reform improved standards but did not end overcrowding. Progress was gradual.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks what cultural motive drove 1920s immigration restriction.

options.text: Plan to abolish all borders
Desire to increase immigration from all regions
Concern that immigrants were too skilled
Nativist fears of cultural and racial change

questions.explanation: Nativist fears of cultural and racial change drove restriction. It was not about increasing immigration or abolishing borders.

questions.stem: A clerk synthesizes the Triangle fire's long-term legacy.

answer.exemplar: It catalyzed workplace safety laws and strengthened labor reform movements in the Progressive Era.

questions.explanation: The fire spurred safety laws and labor reform. Its legacy shaped Progressive Era regulation.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks how factory safety regulation expanded after 1911.

answer.exemplar: State and local codes mandated fire escapes, sprinklers, and inspections, enforced by new labor departments.

questions.explanation: Codes required safety features and inspections. Enforcement came through labor departments.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks what risk installment credit posed to the economy.

options.text: It eliminated all consumer debt
High consumer debt made households vulnerable to income shocks
It guaranteed stable employment
It prevented any consumer purchases

questions.explanation: Installment debt left households vulnerable. It did not eliminate debt or guarantee employment.

questions.stem: A clerk synthesizes how uneven prosperity weakened the economy.

answer.exemplar: Concentrated wealth and weak farm demand limited consumption, contributing to overproduction and instability before 1929.

questions.explanation: Uneven prosperity constrained demand and fueled instability. It was not a sign of broad health.

stimulus.body: A clerk quotes an investor noting that margin calls forced mass selling when prices dipped.

questions.stem: What does that forced selling produce?

options.text: Guaranteed profits for all investors
A stable market equilibrium
A cascading price collapse and panic
Immediate government repayment of losses

questions.explanation: Forced selling cascaded into collapse and panic. It did not stabilize markets or guarantee profits.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks how deposit insurance restored banking confidence.

answer.exemplar: By guaranteeing deposits, it reduced panic withdrawals and stabilized the banking system.

questions.explanation: Insurance reduced panic and stabilized banks. It did not eliminate bank failures entirely.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks what groups Social Security initially excluded.

options.text: No one; coverage was universal
All elderly citizens
Industrial workers entirely
Domestic and agricultural workers

questions.explanation: Initial Social Security excluded domestic and agricultural workers. It did not cover everyone universally.

questions.topic: Deficit spending in the New Deal
questions.stem: A clerk's debate asks what critics of New Deal deficit spending argued.

options.text: It was too small to matter
It would cause inflation and burden future generations
It should have been larger to end the Depression faster
Deficits were impossible under the Constitution

questions.explanation: Critics warned of inflation and future burdens. Supporters wanted more spending; critics did not claim deficits were unconstitutional.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks what FDR's court-packing plan proposed.

answer.exemplar: It proposed adding Supreme Court justices to secure favorable rulings on New Deal legislation.

questions.explanation: The plan expanded the Court to favor New Deal rulings. It failed politically but shifted judicial behavior.

stimulus.body: A clerk quotes a California grower blaming Dust Bowl migrants for low wages and social disorder.

questions.stem: What attitude does that quote reflect?

options.text: Indifference to migration entirely
Warm welcome and full integration
Hostility and scapegoating toward migrants
Government-funded relocation support

questions.explanation: The quote reflects hostility and scapegoating. It does not show welcome or government support.

questions.stem: A clerk's debate asks how war production affected the Depression.

options.text: It abolished all consumer industries permanently
It deepened the Depression immediately
It had no effect on employment
It ended unemployment by mobilizing industry for war

questions.explanation: War production ended unemployment by mobilizing industry. It did not deepen depression or abolish consumer industry.

questions.learningObjective: Analyze the GI Bill's unequal benefits
questions.stem: A clerk's note asks how GI Bill benefits were distributed unequally.

options.text: All veterans received identical benefits without exception
Black veterans often faced discrimination in accessing loans and schools
Only officers received any benefits
No veterans received education benefits

questions.explanation: Black veterans faced discrimination accessing benefits. Coverage was not identical or officer-only.

questions.stem: A clerk synthesizes how wartime work changed women's roles after 1945.

answer.exemplar: Women gained industrial experience and confidence, but postwar norms pushed many back into domestic roles.

questions.explanation: Wartime work empowered women, yet postwar expectations reversed much of that change.

questions.stem: A clerk's debate asks what social effect suburbanization had.

options.text: It eliminated automobile use
It ended all racial segregation nationwide
It reinforced racial segregation and car-dependent living
It abolished private homeownership

questions.explanation: Suburbanization reinforced segregation and car dependence. It did not end segregation or abolish homeownership.

questions.stem: A clerk synthesizes how highways transformed American geography.

answer.exemplar: Interstate highways decentralized population and industry, reshaping cities and enabling suburban sprawl.

questions.explanation: Highways shifted growth outward. They did not concentrate development in urban cores.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks what demographic shift the baby boom created.

options.text: No change in age distribution
An immediate decline in the youth population
A permanent shrinking of the workforce
A large youth cohort that later strained schools and services

questions.explanation: The baby boom created a large youth cohort straining services later. It did not shrink youth or workforce.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks how restrictive covenants were legally challenged.

answer.exemplar: Courts ruled them unenforceable in Shelley v. Kraemer, though segregation persisted through other means.

questions.explanation: Shelley v. Kraemer made covenants unenforceable. Segregation continued by other means.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks why Brown was not immediately implemented.

options.text: The Supreme Court reversed Brown the next year
Massive resistance and local opposition delayed desegregation
All schools desegregated within one year
Brown only applied to private schools

questions.explanation: Massive resistance delayed desegregation. Brown was not reversed or limited to private schools.

questions.stem: A clerk synthesizes the Civil Rights Act of 1964's significance.

answer.exemplar: It dismantled legal segregation in public life and established federal enforcement of equal access.

questions.explanation: The act ended legal segregation and enabled federal enforcement. It did not solve all inequality.

stimulus.body: A clerk quotes a Northern mayor complaining that sudden population growth strained housing and services.

questions.stem: What does that complaint indicate?

options.text: Southern cities absorbed all migrants
Migration had no effect on Northern cities
Rapid migration overwhelmed urban infrastructure
Urban services were universally adequate

questions.explanation: The complaint shows rapid migration strained infrastructure. It did not leave cities unaffected.

questions.stem: A clerk's debate asks whether rising productivity always benefits workers.

options.text: Only in agriculture, never in industry
Always; productivity never harms workers
Never; productivity has no economic value
Not necessarily; gains can accrue to owners while jobs disappear

questions.explanation: Productivity gains may benefit owners and displace workers. They are not automatically or never beneficial.

questions.stem: A clerk synthesizes deindustrialization's impact on Northern cities.

answer.exemplar: Job losses, population decline, and fiscal stress reshaped Northern cities and contributed to urban crisis.

questions.explanation: Deindustrialization brought job loss and fiscal stress. Its effects reshaped urban life.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks what policy dilemma stagflation created.

options.text: It allowed easy simultaneous solutions
Fighting inflation worsened unemployment and vice versa
It eliminated all policy choices
It only affected foreign economies

questions.explanation: Stagflation forced trade-offs between inflation and unemployment. It did not allow easy solutions or only affect foreign economies.

questions.stem: A clerk's debate asks what critics of affirmative action argued.

options.text: It only helped wealthy applicants
It ended all discrimination instantly
It could constitute reverse discrimination
It abolished all college admissions

questions.explanation: Critics argued affirmative action could be reverse discrimination. It did not end all discrimination or abolish admissions.

questions.stem: A clerk synthesizes why 1970s cities faced fiscal crisis.

answer.exemplar: Deindustrialization, suburban flight, and rising service costs combined to strain city budgets.

questions.explanation: Multiple factors strained city budgets. No single cause explains the crisis.

questions.topic: Industrial retention after a plant closing
questions.stem: A clerk's debate asks whether tax incentives reliably retained industry.

options.text: Incentives were illegal in all states
Always; incentives guaranteed permanent retention
Never; incentives had no possible benefit
Not always; firms often left despite incentives

questions.explanation: Incentives did not always retain firms. They were neither universally effective nor illegal.
